variables-assignment.name: Assign and reassign names
variables-assignment.useWhen: you store a value and later replace it
variables-assignment.pitfall: A name keeps its value until a later line assigns again
useCases: Keep a running score that changes each round
Remember the previous value before updating a variable
Swap two values using a temporary name
Count the lives left after each hit
Track the current balance after each deposit
Store a starting value to compare with later

numbers-int-float.name: Whole and decimal numbers
numbers-int-float.useWhen: you divide, convert or round numbers
numbers-int-float.template:
<a> / <b>        # always a float
int(<x>)         # drops the decimals
round(<x>, <digits>)
numbers-int-float.pitfall: / always gives a float; int() cuts, never rounds
useCases: Split a bill evenly between friends
Average a list of test scores
Convert minutes to hours with decimals
Show a price rounded to two decimals
Turn a decimal rating into whole stars
Check whether two measured lengths are close enough

integer-division-modulo.name: Floor division and remainder
integer-division-modulo.useWhen: you need whole groups and what is left over
integer-division-modulo.pitfall: // floors toward minus infinity, so negatives go down
useCases: Turn total minutes into hours and minutes
Split players into full teams and leftovers
Check whether a number is even
Get the last digit of a number
Wrap a clock hour past twelve
Find which row a grid cell index falls in

str-vs-number.name: Text versus number values
str-vs-number.useWhen: values come from input, files or text fields
str-vs-number.rule: Quotes make text; + joins text but adds numbers.
str-vs-number.howItRuns: '2' + '3' joins two strings into '23'; int('2') + int('3') converts first, then adds to 5.
str-vs-number.pitfall: Digits in quotes are text: convert with int() first
useCases: Add two numbers typed in by a user
Build an order code from digit strings
Sort version numbers stored as text
Total prices read from a CSV file
Pad a number with zeros for an ID
Compare ages entered as text

string-indexing.name: Index into a string
string-indexing.useWhen: you need one character at a known position
string-indexing.pitfall: Positions start at 0, and the last is len - 1
useCases: Get the first letter of a name for initials
Check whether a word ends with a vowel
Read the check digit at the end of a code
Compare the first and last letters of a word
Find the middle character of a string
Show the second letter of a password hint

string-methods.name: Call string methods
string-methods.useWhen: you need a changed copy of some text
string-methods.pitfall: Methods return a new string; the original never changes
useCases: Clean spaces from a name typed by a user
Make a search ignore capital letters with lower()
Replace every comma with a semicolon
Check whether a file name ends with .py
Turn a title into upper case for a heading
Count how many times a letter appears

comparison-equality.name: Compare values
comparison-equality.useWhen: you order or match values, including text
comparison-equality.pitfall: Text compares letter by letter, and capitals come first
useCases: Sort names alphabetically before printing
Check whether a typed answer matches the key
Find the earliest word in a list
Compare a stored ID with a typed one
Check that a score beats the high score
Match a command name ignoring capital letters

conditionals.name: Branch with if and else
conditionals.useWhen: the program must choose between different actions
conditionals.pitfall: Only the first true branch of an if/elif chain runs
useCases: Give a letter grade from a test score
Show a warning when the battery is low
Pick free, standard or express shipping by weight
Say whether a number is negative, zero or positive
Greet the user by time of day
Apply a discount only to members

booleans-truthiness.name: Truthy and falsy values
booleans-truthiness.useWhen: you test a value directly in an if or while
booleans-truthiness.rule: Empty, zero and None are false; everything else is true.
booleans-truthiness.howItRuns: if x: calls bool(x); [], '', 0 and None give False, so '0' and [0] count as true.
booleans-truthiness.pitfall: '0', ' ' and [0] are not empty, so they are true
useCases: Skip blank lines when reading a file
Show a default name when the input is empty
Stop a loop when the queue runs out
Check whether any search results came back
Use a fallback value with or
Warn when a shopping cart is empty

for-range-bounds.name: Count with a range loop
for-range-bounds.useWhen: you repeat something a known number of times
for-range-bounds.template:
for <i> in range(<start>, <stop>):
    <body>    # stop is excluded
for-range-bounds.pitfall: range stops just before the stop value
useCases: Print a times table from 1 to 10
Repeat a greeting three times
Visit every index of a list
Count down from 10 to 1
Take every second number up to 20
Number the lines of a report starting at 1

loop-accumulator.name: Accumulate in a loop
loop-accumulator.useWhen: you need one result built from every item
loop-accumulator.pitfall: Set the starting value once, before the loop
useCases: Add up the prices in a shopping cart
Count the words longer than five letters
Find the highest temperature of the week
Join names into one comma-separated string
Multiply all the numbers in a list together
Total the minutes of a playlist

while-loop-termination.name: Loop until a condition
while-loop-termination.useWhen: you repeat until something changes, count unknown
while-loop-termination.pitfall: The condition is checked only before each pass
useCases: Halve a number until it drops below one
Keep asking until the answer is valid
Pay off a loan month by month
Count the digits of a number
Double savings until they reach a goal
Serve customers until the queue is empty

break-continue.name: Exit or skip iterations
break-continue.useWhen: a loop should stop early or skip some items
break-continue.pitfall: break leaves only the innermost loop
useCases: Stop reading at the first blank line
Skip comment lines that start with #
Find the first negative number and stop
Ignore invalid entries while summing
Stop a game loop when the player quits
Search a grid row by row for a target

list-indexing.name: Index into a list
list-indexing.useWhen: you need one item at a known position
list-indexing.pitfall: Index 0 is first; the last index is len - 1
useCases: Get the winner from the front of a ranked list
Read the newest entry at the end of a log
Replace the third score after a regrade
Swap the first and last items
Look up a month name by its number
Read the middle value of a sorted list

list-slicing.name: Slice a sequence
list-slicing.useWhen: you need a run of items from a list or string
list-slicing.pitfall: The item at the stop index is never included
useCases: Take the first three scores from a list
Drop the header row from a list of lines
Get the last two characters of a file name
Keep a list without its first and last items
Split a list into a first half and a second half
Read every second item of a list
Reverse a string in one step

list-mutation-methods.name: Change a list in place
list-mutation-methods.useWhen: you add, remove or reorder items in an existing list
list-mutation-methods.pitfall: append and sort return None; they change the list itself
useCases: Add a new message to a chat history
Remove the most recent undo step
Sort a leaderboard in place

alias-copy.name: Aliases share one object
alias-copy.useWhen: two names might point at the same list or dict
alias-copy.rule: Assignment never copies: both names share one object.
alias-copy.howItRuns: b = a makes b another name for the same list; changes through either name show in both.
alias-copy.pitfall: Copy with .copy() before changing a list you must keep

Pass a list to a function without it being changed
Store snapshots of a list for an undo history
Build a grid whose rows change independently
Reset a game board to its starting layout
Compare a list before and after editing it

string-split-join.name: Split and join text
string-split-join.useWhen: you turn text into pieces, or pieces into text
string-split-join.pitfall: split keeps empty pieces; join needs strings only
useCases: Break a CSV line into fields
Split a sentence into words
Rebuild a date with dashes instead of slashes
Join a list of names with commas
Turn a list of numbers into one line of text
Count the words in a title

dict-access-missing-key.name: Look up a key safely
dict-access-missing-key.useWhen: a key might be missing from a dictionary
dict-access-missing-key.pitfall: d[key] raises KeyError when the key is missing

Read an optional setting with a default
Check whether a username is taken
Translate a word if it is in the glossary
Show zero stock for an unknown product
Find a phone number by name safely

counting-with-dict.name: Count with a dictionary
counting-with-dict.useWhen: you need how many times each value appears
counting-with-dict.pitfall: Create the dict once, before the loop
useCases: Count how often each word appears in a text
Tally votes for each candidate
Count letters to check for anagrams
Find the most common error code in a log

Count how many students got each grade

function-def-call.name: Define and call a function
function-def-call.useWhen: you will run the same steps more than once
function-def-call.pitfall: def only defines; nothing runs until you call with ()

Compute a rectangle's area for several rooms
Convert many temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit
Format a price the same way everywhere
Check several passwords with one rule
Draw a border line above and below a title

function-return-vs-print.name: Return a value, not print
function-return-vs-print.useWhen: a function's result is needed by other code
function-return-vs-print.pitfall: print only shows a value; return hands it back

Check a password and use the answer in an if
Convert a temperature and store the result

reading-tracebacks.name: Read a traceback
reading-tracebacks.useWhen: a program crashed and you need to find why
reading-tracebacks.template:
Read bottom up: the error type and message,
then the last frame: its line and code
reading-tracebacks.pitfall: The last frame shows where it failed, not always the bug
useCases: Find which line raised an IndexError
Tell a typo NameError from a missing import
See which call passed a bad value into a helper
Spot a KeyError from a misspelled dictionary key
Find where a None value was used by mistake
Explain a ZeroDivisionError in an average function

transforms.belief: Changing {{@a}} later also changes {{@b}}
transforms.refutation: {{@b}} = {{@a}} gave {{@b}} the value {{@a}} had at that moment; a new value for {{@a}} later does not reach {{@b}}.
transforms.rule: Assignment copies the current value; later changes do not follow.

transforms.belief: The first print already shows the updated {{@a}}
transforms.refutation: Lines run top to bottom: when the first print runs, the line that changes {{@a}} has not run yet.
transforms.rule: Each print shows the values as they are at that line.

transforms.belief: These two lines swap {{@a}} and {{@b}}
transforms.refutation: After {{@a}} = {{@b}}, the old value of {{@a}} is gone, so {{@b}} = {{@a}} copies the new value straight back.
transforms.rule: Swapping needs a temporary name, or a, b = b, a.

transforms.belief: {{@copy}} also gets the new ending
transforms.refutation: {{@copy}} was given the text {{@name}} held at that moment; building a new text for {{@name}} leaves {{@copy}} unchanged.
transforms.rule: Assignment copies the current value; later changes do not follow.

transforms.belief: {{@total}} / {{p}} gives a whole number
transforms.refutation: The / operator always gives a float, even for two whole numbers that divide evenly; only // gives a whole number.
transforms.rule: / always returns a float; // gives a whole number.

transforms.belief: int() rounds {{@share}} to the nearest whole number
transforms.refutation: int() simply cuts off everything after the decimal point; it never rounds up.
transforms.rule: int() drops the decimals; round() rounds.

transforms.belief: Dividing two whole numbers by 2 gives a whole number
transforms.refutation: The / operator always gives a float, even for two whole numbers that divide evenly; only // gives a whole number.
transforms.rule: / always returns a float; // gives a whole number.

transforms.belief: {{@a}} + {{@b}} is exactly 0.{{s}}
transforms.refutation: Decimals like these are stored in binary as tiny approximations, so their sum is a hair off and == fails.
transforms.rule: Floats are approximate: compare with a tolerance, never ==.

transforms.belief: round() always rounds a half up
transforms.refutation: Python rounds an exact half to the nearest even whole number, so some halves go down and some go up.
transforms.rule: round() sends exact halves to the even neighbour.

check({{@fn}}([{{a}}, {{b}}]) == {{m}}, 'mean of two values')
check({{@fn}}([]) == 0.0, 'an empty list gives 0.0')
check(type({{@fn}}([2, 4])) == float, 'the mean is always a float')

templates.rule: / always returns a float; // floors to a whole number.

transforms.belief: {{@total}} // 60 rounds to the nearest minute
transforms.refutation: // always rounds down to the whole number below, even when the leftover is more than half.
transforms.rule: // rounds down; it never rounds to the nearest.

transforms.belief: % 60 gives how many times 60 fits
transforms.refutation: % gives what is left over after taking out whole sixties; // is the one that counts them.
transforms.rule: % gives the remainder; // gives how many times.

transforms.belief: // on a negative number just drops the decimals
transforms.refutation: // rounds down toward minus infinity, so a negative result moves further from zero, not toward it.
transforms.rule: // floors: negative results round away from zero.

transforms.belief: {{@delta}} % {{b}} gives a negative remainder
transforms.refutation: In Python the remainder takes the sign of the divisor, so % by a positive number is never negative.
transforms.rule: % by a positive number is never negative.

transforms.belief: % 10 gives how many tens are in {{@n}}
transforms.refutation: % gives the remainder after dividing, which here is the last digit; // counts the tens.
transforms.rule: % gives the remainder; // gives how many times.

transforms.belief: {{@n}} // 10 rounds to the nearest ten
transforms.refutation: // always rounds down to the whole number below, even when the leftover is more than half.
transforms.rule: // rounds down; it never rounds to the nearest.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}(125) == '2:05', '125 minutes is 2:05')
check({{@fn}}({{m}}) == '{{h}}:{{r}}', 'whole hours, then the minutes left over')

templates.rule: // always rounds down, never to the nearest.

transforms.belief: {{@a}} + {{@b}} adds the two numbers
transforms.refutation: Both values are in quotes, so they are strings; + on strings glues the text together.
transforms.rule: + joins strings; convert with int() to add.

transforms.belief: {{@a}} * {{k}} multiplies the number
transforms.refutation: A string times a whole number repeats the text that many times; it does no arithmetic.
transforms.rule: A string times n repeats the text n times.

transforms.belief: '{{x}}' and '{{y}}' compare as numbers
transforms.refutation: Strings compare character by character from the left, so the first digits decide, not the size of the number.
transforms.rule: Text compares character by character, not by numeric size.

transforms.belief: {{@count}} + {{@extra}} does the arithmetic
transforms.refutation: Python refuses to add a number and a string; it raises an error instead of guessing which you meant.
transforms.rule: Mixing a number and a string with + raises TypeError.

templates.rule: + joins strings; convert with int() to add numbers.

check({{@fn}}('{{a}},{{b}}') == {{s}}, 'adds the numbers written in the text')

transforms.belief: Index {{i}} is letter number {{i}}, counting from 1
transforms.refutation: Positions count from zero, so each index here is one letter further along than counting from one suggests.
transforms.rule: Index 0 is the first character.

transforms.belief: {{@word}}[-1] is an error
transforms.refutation: Negative indexes count back from the end of the string, so -1 means the last character.
transforms.rule: Index -1 is the last character.

transforms.belief: {{@name}}[{{@n}} - 1] is the second-to-last letter
transforms.refutation: The last character sits at index len minus one, because counting starts at zero.
transforms.rule: The last index is len - 1.

transforms.belief: {{@word}}[0] = '{{c}}' changes the first letter
transforms.refutation: Strings cannot be changed in place; to get a different word you must build a new string.
transforms.rule: Strings are immutable: build a new one instead.

transforms.belief: {{@code}}[len({{@code}})] is the last character
transforms.refutation: Indexes run from zero to len minus one, so position len is one past the end.
transforms.rule: The last index is len - 1.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}(['Ada', 'Lovelace']) == 'AL', 'initials of Ada Lovelace')
check({{@fn}}(['{{n1}}', '{{f1}}', '{{c1}}']) == '{{n1}}'[0] + '{{f1}}'[0] + '{{c1}}'[0], 'one letter per word')

templates.rule: Index 0 is the first character.

transforms.belief: {{@tag}}.upper() changes {{@tag}} itself
transforms.refutation: String methods return a new string; without assigning the result back, {{@tag}} still holds the original text.
transforms.rule: String methods return new text; assign it to keep it.

transforms.belief: replace changes only the first '{{f}}'
transforms.refutation: replace swaps every match in the string unless you pass a count as a third argument.
transforms.rule: replace changes every match unless given a count.

transforms.belief: replace also changes {{@s}} itself
transforms.refutation: {{@s}} is never changed: replace builds a new string, and only {{@t}} holds it.
transforms.rule: String methods return new text; assign it to keep it.

transforms.belief: strip('-') also removes the dashes between the words
transforms.refutation: strip only trims characters at the two ends; the ones between words stay where they are.
transforms.rule: strip() trims the ends only, never the middle.

transforms.belief: upper() changes {{@raw}} itself
transforms.refutation: upper returns a new string; the line throws that result away, so {{@raw}} keeps its original letters.
transforms.rule: String methods return new text; assign it to keep it.

templates.harness:

check({{@fn}}([' {{n1}}  ']) == ['{{n1}}'.lower()], 'one padded name')

transforms.belief: Shorter words count as smaller when comparing text
transforms.refutation: Strings compare letter by letter from the left, like a dictionary; length only matters when one word is a prefix.
transforms.rule: Text compares alphabetically, letter by letter, not by length.

transforms.belief: Capital letters count as bigger than small letters
transforms.refutation: Every capital letter sorts before every small letter, so a capitalised word compares as smaller.
transforms.rule: Capitals sort before lowercase letters.

transforms.belief: The number {{@stock}} equals the text '{{n}}'
transforms.refutation: A number never equals a string in Python, even when the digits look the same; convert one side first.
transforms.rule: A number never equals a string; convert before comparing.

transforms.belief: Both true branches run, one after the other
transforms.refutation: An if/elif chain stops at the first true condition; the later branches are skipped even if they are also true.
transforms.rule: Only the first true branch of an if/elif chain runs.

transforms.belief: Only one of the two ifs can run
transforms.refutation: These are two separate if statements, not an if/elif chain, so each condition is checked on its own.
transforms.rule: Separate ifs are each checked; only elif chains are exclusive.

transforms.belief: This checks {{@pet}} against both '{{a}}' and '{{b}}'
transforms.refutation: or joins two separate tests; the second one is just a non-empty string, which always counts as true.
transforms.rule: Repeat the variable: x == 'a' or x == 'b'.

transforms.belief: An empty list like {{@a}} counts as true
transforms.refutation: Python treats every empty container as false; only a list with at least one item is true.
transforms.rule: Empty lists, strings and zero are false.

transforms.belief: The text '0' counts as false
transforms.refutation: {{@b}} is a one-character string, and any non-empty string is true; only the number zero is false.
transforms.rule: Any non-empty string is true, even '0'.

transforms.belief: {{@given}} or '{{w}}' gives True or False
transforms.refutation: or returns one of its operands: the first true one, here the fallback text, not a boolean.

transforms.refutation: and returns the last value it looked at when all are true, so the result is a number, not a boolean.

transforms.belief: The empty list {{@cart}} counts as true in the if
transforms.refutation: Python treats every empty container as false; only a list with at least one item is true.
transforms.rule: Empty lists, strings and zero are false.

transforms.belief: The text '0' in {{@code}} counts as false
transforms.refutation: {{@code}} holds a one-character string, and any non-empty string is true; only the number zero is false.
transforms.rule: Any non-empty string is true, even '0'.

templates.rule: An empty list is false; a list with items is true.

transforms.belief: continue ends the whole loop, like break
transforms.refutation: continue only skips the rest of this pass; the loop goes on with the next item.
transforms.rule: continue skips one pass; break ends the loop.

transforms.belief: break skips only the negative item, then the loop goes on
transforms.refutation: break ends the whole loop at once; the items after it are never visited.
transforms.rule: break ends the loop; continue skips one item.

transforms.belief: The else part runs after break too
transforms.refutation: A loop's else runs only when the loop finishes without break; here break fires, so the else is skipped.
transforms.rule: A loop else runs only if no break happened.

transforms.belief: break also stops the outer loop over the words
transforms.refutation: break leaves only the loop it is directly inside; the outer loop moves on to the next word.
transforms.rule: break exits only the innermost loop.

transforms.belief: break skips only the vowel, then the letters go on
transforms.refutation: break ends the inner loop at the first vowel; the letters after it are never printed.
transforms.rule: break ends the loop; continue skips one item.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}(['a', '# note', 'b', 'END', 'c']) == ['a', 'b'], 'skips comments and stops at END')
check({{@fn}}(['{{w1}}', 'END', '{{w2}}']) == ['{{w1}}'], 'nothing after END')
check({{@fn}}(['# x', '{{w2}}']) == ['{{w2}}'], 'a comment is skipped, not the rest')

templates.rule: break ends the loop; continue skips one item.

transforms.belief: {{@xs}}[{{i}}] is item number {{i}}, counting from 1
transforms.refutation: List positions count from zero, so [{{i}}] is one place further along than you would count by hand.
transforms.rule: Index 0 is the first item.

transforms.belief: {{@xs}}[-1] raises an error
transforms.refutation: Negative indexes count back from the end, so -1 picks the last item.
transforms.rule: Index -1 is the last item.

transforms.belief: {{@xs}}[{{@n}} - 1] is the second-to-last item
transforms.refutation: With {{@n}} items the positions run from zero to {{@n}} minus one, so that index is the last one.
transforms.rule: The last index is len - 1.

transforms.belief: {{@xs}}[{{i}}] is item number {{i}}, counting from 1
transforms.refutation: List positions count from zero, so [{{i}}] is one place further along than you would count by hand.
transforms.rule: Index 0 is the first item.

transforms.belief: {{@xs}}[-{{k}}] raises an error
transforms.refutation: Negative indexes count back from the end of the list, so -{{k}} is a valid position, not an error.
transforms.rule: Negative indexes count from the end.

transforms.belief: {{@xs}}[len({{@xs}})] is the last item
transforms.refutation: Positions run from zero to len minus one, so len itself is one step past the end.
transforms.rule: The last index is len - 1.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}([1, 2, 3]) == [3, 2, 1], 'swaps the two ends')
check({{@fn}}([{{a}}, {{b}}]) == [{{b}}, {{a}}], 'two items trade places')
check({{@fn}}([{{a}}]) == [{{a}}], 'one item stays')

templates.rule: Index 0 is the first item.

transforms.belief: The slice includes the item at the stop index
transforms.refutation: The stop index is left out: [{{i}}:{{j}}] takes the items at indexes {{i}} up to, but not including, {{j}}.
transforms.rule: A slice includes the start index and excludes the stop.

transforms.belief: The first item is at position 1, not 0
transforms.refutation: Indexes count from zero: the first item is index zero, so index {{i}} is one item further along.
transforms.rule: Index 0 is the first item.

transforms.belief: Changing {{@part}} also changes {{@xs}}
transforms.refutation: A slice builds a brand-new list, so assigning into {{@part}} leaves {{@xs}} untouched.
transforms.rule: A slice is a copy; changing it never touches the original.

transforms.belief: {{@xs}}[:{{k}}] includes the item at index {{k}}
transforms.refutation: The stop index is left out, so [:{{k}}] takes exactly {{k}} items.
transforms.rule: A slice includes the start index and excludes the stop.

transforms.belief: Slicing up to {{big}}, past the end, raises an error
transforms.refutation: A slice quietly stops at the end of the list; only indexing a single missing position raises an error.
transforms.rule: Slices clip to the list's end; they never raise.

transforms.belief: The slice starts at item number {{i}}, counting from 1
transforms.refutation: Positions count from zero, so index {{i}} is one item further along than counting from one suggests.
transforms.rule: Index 0 is the first item.

transforms.belief: Each slice includes the letter at its stop index
transforms.refutation: The stop index is left out: each slice ends just before the position written after the colon.
transforms.rule: A slice includes the start index and excludes the stop.

transforms.belief: Position {{i}} is letter number {{i}}, counting from 1
transforms.refutation: Positions count from zero, so index {{i}} is one letter further along than counting from one suggests.
transforms.rule: Index 0 is the first character.

templates.rule: A slice stops just before its stop index.

transforms.belief: {{@xs}}.append({{n}}) gives back the updated list
transforms.refutation: append changes {{@xs}} in place and hands back nothing, so {{@ys}} is not a list.
transforms.rule: append changes the list and returns None.

transforms.belief: Appending [{{a}}, {{b}}] adds {{a}} and {{b}} as separate items
transforms.refutation: append always adds exactly one item; here that item is a whole list, nested inside.
transforms.rule: append adds one item; extend adds each item.

transforms.belief: pop() removes the first item
transforms.refutation: With no argument, pop takes the item at the end of the list, like the top of a stack.
transforms.rule: pop() removes the last item; pop(0) the first.

transforms.belief: {{@stack}}.sort() gives back the sorted list
transforms.refutation: sort reorders the list in place and returns nothing, so {{@result}} is not a list.
transforms.rule: sort() sorts in place and returns None; sorted() returns a list.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}([3, 1], 2) == [1, 2, 3], 'adds the item and sorts')
check({{@fn}}([{{b}}, {{a}}], {{c}}) == [{{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}}], 'keeps the list in order')
check({{@fn}}([{{a}}], {{a}}) == [{{a}}], 'no duplicate')

templates.rule: sort() returns None; sorted() returns a new list.

transforms.belief: {{@b}} = {{@a}} makes {{@b}} a separate copy
transforms.refutation: Assignment never copies a list: {{@b}} and {{@a}} are two names for one list, so the append shows through both.
transforms.rule: b = a shares one list; use a.copy() for a new one.

transforms.belief: Pointing {{@a}} at a new list also changes {{@b}}
transforms.refutation: This line makes {{@a}} name a brand-new list; {{@b}} still names the old one, which nobody changed.
transforms.rule: Rebinding a name never changes other names; mutating does.

transforms.belief: {{@fn}} works on its own copy of {{@xs}}
transforms.refutation: The parameter {{@items}} is just another name for the caller's list, so the append changes {{@xs}} too.
transforms.rule: Functions receive the same list, not a copy.

transforms.belief: {{@grid}}.copy() also copies the inner lists
transforms.refutation: copy() makes a new outer list, but its rows are the same inner lists, so changing a row shows in both.
transforms.rule: .copy() is shallow: inner lists are still shared.

templates.rule: b = a shares one list; a.copy() makes a new one.

given = [3, 1]
check({{@fn}}(given, 2) == [1, 2, 3], 'adds the item and sorts')

check({{@fn}}([{{b}}], {{a}}) == [{{a}}, {{b}}], 'a one-item list')

transforms.belief: Each piece keeps its dash after splitting
transforms.refutation: split cuts at each separator and throws the separators away, so no piece contains one.
transforms.rule: split removes the separator from every piece.

transforms.belief: Splitting skips the empty pieces between commas
transforms.refutation: Every comma marks a cut, so two commas in a row, or one at the end, leave empty strings.
transforms.rule: split with a separator keeps the empty pieces.

transforms.belief: Each piece keeps its comma after splitting
transforms.refutation: split cuts at each separator and throws the separators away, so no piece contains one.
transforms.rule: split removes the separator from every piece.

transforms.belief: join also puts '{{sep}}' after the last word
transforms.refutation: join puts the separator only between items, so there is one fewer separator than items.
transforms.rule: join puts the separator between items, never at the end.

transforms.belief: join can glue a list of numbers together
transforms.refutation: join only accepts strings; each number must be turned into text first, for example with str().
transforms.rule: join needs strings: convert numbers with str() first.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}('a, b,c') == 'a | b | c', 'three fields')
check({{@fn}}('{{w1}} ,{{w2}}') == '{{w1}} | {{w2}}', 'two fields')

templates.rule: join puts the separator only between items.

transforms.belief: {{@d}}['{{@k3}}'] gives None when the key is missing
transforms.refutation: Square brackets demand the key; when it is missing Python raises an error. Only get hands back a fallback.
transforms.rule: d[key] raises KeyError if missing; d.get(key) does not.

transforms.belief: get with a default also stores '{{@k3}}' in {{@d}}
transforms.refutation: get only reads: it hands back the default for a missing key without adding anything to the dictionary.
transforms.rule: get(key, default) reads only; it never adds the key.

transforms.belief: in checks the values of {{@d}}, not its keys
transforms.refutation: in on a dictionary looks only at its keys; use values() to search the values.
transforms.rule: key in d checks the keys only.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}({'tea': 2, 'pie': 5}, ['tea', 'pie', 'tea']) == 9, 'adds the listed prices')
check({{@fn}}({'tea': 2}, ['tea', 'cake']) == 2, 'unknown items cost 0')
check({{@fn}}({'{{f}}': {{a}}}, ['{{f}}', '{{f}}']) == {{a2}}, 'the same item twice')

templates.rule: d[key] raises KeyError for a missing key; get does not.

transforms.belief: {{@seen}}[{{@w}}] = 1 adds one each time {{@w}} appears
transforms.refutation: Assigning a fixed value overwrites whatever was there, so a repeated word never counts any higher.
transforms.rule: Add to the old count: counts.get(w, 0) + 1.

transforms.belief: += 1 works before {{@w}} is a key
transforms.refutation: += first reads the current count, and reading a key that is not there yet raises an error.
transforms.rule: Give a new key a start value, for example with get.

transforms.belief: {{@counts}} keeps the earlier counts across passes
transforms.refutation: {{@counts}} = {} inside the loop throws the dictionary away on every pass, so only the last word survives.
transforms.rule: Create the counting dict once, before the loop.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}(['a', 'B', 'b']) == {'a': 1, 'b': 2}, 'counts, ignoring case')
check({{@fn}}([]) == {}, 'nothing to count')
check({{@fn}}(['{{x}}', '{{x}}', '{{x}}']) == {'{{x}}': 3}, 'one word three times')

templates.rule: Add one to the old count; = 1 just resets it.

transforms.belief: Defining {{@fn}} already runs its body
transforms.refutation: def only stores the function; its body runs each time {{@fn}}() is called, which happens on the last line.
transforms.rule: A function body runs only when the function is called.

transforms.belief: {{@x}} = {{@fn}} calls {{@fn}} and stores its result
transforms.refutation: Without parentheses nothing is called: {{@x}} just becomes another name for the function itself.
transforms.rule: Only name() calls a function; the bare name is the function.

transforms.belief: Arguments match parameters with the same names, whatever the order
transforms.refutation: Arguments are matched by position: the first value goes to the first parameter, whatever the caller's variable is called.
transforms.rule: Positional arguments fill parameters in order, ignoring names.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}(3, 4) == 25, '3*3 + 4*4')
check({{@fn}}({{p}}, {{q}}) == {{r}}, 'squares both values, then adds')

templates.rule: Only name() runs the function.

transforms.belief: Printing {{@x}} * {{k}} also hands the value back to {{@r}}
transforms.refutation: print only shows text on screen; a function without return gives back nothing, so {{@r}} receives no value.
transforms.rule: Only return sends a value back to the caller.

transforms.belief: The greeting printed inside {{@fn}} is also returned
transforms.refutation: print only shows text on screen; {{@fn}} has no return line, so {{@msg}} receives no value.
transforms.rule: Only return sends a value back to the caller.

transforms.belief: return shows the value on the screen
transforms.refutation: return hands the value back silently; the bare call on the third line throws it away without showing it.
transforms.rule: Returned values appear only if you print them.

transforms.belief: The print after return still runs
transforms.refutation: return ends the function immediately; any line after it in the same block is never reached.
transforms.rule: Nothing after return runs.

transforms.belief: return inside the loop only ends that pass
transforms.refutation: return leaves the whole function at once, in the middle of the first pass; the loop never gets a second turn.
transforms.rule: return exits the function, ending any loop inside it.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}([1, 7, 9], 5) == 7, 'the first value above 5')
check({{@fn}}([{{a}}, {{b}}], {{lim}}) == {{b}}, 'skips values at or below the limit')
check({{@fn}}([1, 2], 5) is None, 'nothing above the limit')

templates.rule: print shows a value; only return hands it back.
